source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages
source.authors: Lyzander Marciano Andrylie; Inaya Rahmanisa; Mahardika Krisna Ihsani; A. Wicaksono; H. Wibowo; Alham Fikri Aji

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses language-specific neurons as a baseline for language identification and steering, but does not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated concepts or how common such neurons are.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions neuron polysemanticity as motivation, citing prior work. Its own experiments identify language-specific neurons/features and evaluate language identification and multilingual behavior; these do not test the claim versions about polysemanticity. Neuron-based language-identification results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. The PPL steering matrices evaluate multilingual functionality, not polysemanticity, and are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper cites neuron polysemanticity (Elhage et al. 2022) only as motivation for using SAEs. Its own experiments find language-specific SAE features, steer with them, and use them for language identification. Language-specific neurons appear only as a baseline. No result measures how often neurons respond to unrelated inputs, or what causes or modulates this. The claim that features give 'more isolated' PPL effects than neurons is an indirect comparison of steering selectivity, not a polysemanticity rate. Note that T4 requires using the finding as a tool, and the study does not do that.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that language-specific SAE features exist, sit mainly in middle-to-late layers, and are interpretable. They affect perplexity and output language, and support interpretable language identification near fastText. Neuron polysemanticity is assumed from prior work, not measured.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts LAPE to identify language-specific SAE features and uses language-specific neurons as a comparison; it does not reproduce the methods of the cited original sources for the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that LID performance and steering effects vary across model families; its explanation attributes some LID differences to feature-count bias and the TopK versus JumpReLU activation constraints.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering language-specific SAE features with alpha=-0.2 mostly raises target-language perplexity. The authors say this is more isolated than steering language-specific neurons, attributing the difference to features' 'greater monosemanticity' (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features give more language-selective causal effects than LAPE-selected neurons in Llama 3.2 1B.

fits_no_version.finding: Classifiers built on language-specific neurons score lower than SAE-feature classifiers and fastText on WiLI-2018, much lower in Llama 3.2 1B (F1 0.528).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-specific neuron activation counts are a weaker language identifier than SAE features in Llama 3.2 1B.

record.problems: The reported neuron-classifier results concern language identification rather than polysemanticity. The paper’s interpretation evaluation uses an automated LLM pipeline; the authors note that interpretations based on top-activating examples may miss weaker activations. The study’s LID discussion also notes language-count bias and weaker performance for some languages/models.
record.rows_left_out: PPL steering matrices (Figure 6 and Figures 26–32) are not extracted: they report multilingual functionality effects of language-specific neuron interventions, not whether neurons respond to unrelated concepts. The generated-text steering counts are likewise not measures of neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: All parts; no vision models are studied.
The share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens, and how it varies by layer. Only language-specific neuron counts per layer are reported.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
Effects of architecture, activation function or regularization on the neuron polysemanticity share.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons turn out to detect a shared feature.
Whether polysemanticity classification depends on activation range or explanation scoring for neurons. The paper notes for SAE features only that top-activation explanations lower recall.

record.verdict_notes: Relation was changed from uses_without_test/T4 to cites_only/T6. Polysemanticity appears only as cited motivation, and the neuron baseline is not a test of any version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether transformer MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how the share varies by layer.
Whether superposition or capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure, including effects of initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Changes in the share of polysemantic neurons due to activation, architecture, or regularization, and performance costs of reducing it.
Whether apparently polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs when examined with better tools.
Whether polysemanticity classification depends on activation range or explanation scoring.
